stops.name: Aachen, the Palatine Chapel: with his own hands he crowns Louis
stops.campa: The emperor summons Louis from Aquitaine, and on the eleventh of September, in the octagon, wearing his crown, he leads his last son to the altar where a second crown lies. No pope is present; none has been invited. He asks the people if it pleases them (they cry that it is God's will), and the emperor with his own hands sets the crown on Louis and names him consort of the imperial name. The lesson of Christmas 800 is delivered back to history: the empire of the Franks crowns itself. The octagon holds them both under its dome like two figures in one reliquary.
stops.quote: He placed a crown upon his head and made him partner in the imperial name.

stops.name: Aachen, the last winter: fever, the seventh day
stops.campa: In January, after the autumn's hunting, a high fever takes him in the bath-warm palace, and he doctors himself as he always has, by fasting, believing illness can be starved like a besieged town. Pleurisy settles into the side of the swimmer of Aachen. He keeps to his bed and takes almost nothing but a little water. The court moves on tiptoe through halls built for his stride. On the seventh day he asks for his chaplain and receives the holy communion; those at the bedside see him gathering himself, deliberately, as for one more crossing of the Alps.

stops.name: Aachen, the death of the emperor
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of January, at nine in the morning, having received the sacrament, Charles dies in the seventy-second year of his life and the forty-seventh of his reign. He signs himself, they say, with the cross, composes his own limbs on the bed, and sings under his breath the verse: into thy hands I commend my spirit. The news goes out from Aachen like a change of weather over the whole of the West; Louis comes from Aquitaine to an empire already draped. Einhard, who loved him, writes the date with a clerk's plainness and lets the plainness carry the grief.
stops.quote: He died January twenty-eighth, the seventh day from the time that he took to his bed, at nine o'clock in the morning, after partaking of the holy communion, in the seventy-second year of his age and the forty-seventh of his reign.

stops.name: The Palatine Chapel, the entombment and the golden epitaph
stops.campa: He had named no burial place; all agree none could be more fitting than the basilica he built. He is buried the same day he died: washed, cared for, carried into the octagon amid the greatest lamentation of the whole people, and laid beneath a gilded arch with his image above, and the inscription set in gold letters: here lies the body of Charles, the great and orthodox emperor, who nobly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks and reigned prosperously forty-seven years. The dome he raised closes over him. The word MAGNUS enters the grave with him and never leaves the language again.
stops.quote: Sub hoc conditorio situm est corpus Karoli, Magni atque Orthodoxi Imperatoris, qui regnum Francorum nobiliter ampliavit et per annos XLVII feliciter rexit.

stops.name: The vault beneath the octagon, the emperor seated in the tomb
stops.campa: And this is what the register keeps beneath the pavement: the emperor does not lie down. The tradition seats him in the vault on a throne as one living: crowned with gold, sceptred, girt with the sword, the pilgrim's scrip of Compostela at his side, and on his knees the Gospel, open, his gloved finger at the page. The tomb is sealed and filled with treasures and spices, and the seated king begins his long audience in the dark: the emperor who does not die but waits, the sleeping king of the mountain before there was a mountain, holding the Word open at the place where he stopped reading.

stops.name: Aachen, Otto III opens the vault in the year 1000
stops.campa: At Pentecost of the millennial year Emperor Otto III has the pavement of the chapel broken and goes down with Count Otto of Lomello into the vault. They find him as the register promised: not lying as the dead lie, but seated on a throne as if alive, the golden crown on the skull, the sceptre in gloved hands, and the fingernails, grown on in death, have pierced through the gloves. Nothing has fallen away but the tip of the nose, which Otto restores in gold. He clothes the dead emperor in white, cuts the nails, takes one tooth for a relic, and seals the tomb.
stops.quote: He was not lying, as the bodies of other dead men lie, but sat upon a throne as though living, crowned with a golden crown, holding a sceptre in gloved hands, through which his fingernails had grown and pierced.
stops.quote_source: Chronicon Novaliciense III.32 (the account of Count Otto of Lomello)

stops.name: Aachen, the canonization of the emperor
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of December 1165, at the urging of Frederick Barbarossa, the bones are raised from the vault and Charles is enrolled among the saints of God, Sanctus Karolus, Aachen decked for the elevation, the imperial court attending its own ancestor onto the altars. The emperor of the Franks becomes a saint of the empire he made, his relics parted into arm and skull reliquaries of gold, his cult kept at Aachen. The kingdom he anointed returns the favor: France's kings march under Saint Charlemagne, and Joan of Orleans names him among the saints of the kingdom she will call holy.

stops.name: Aachen, the last nail: the emperor sealed in the golden shrine
stops.campa: Two days after his own crowning at Aachen, Frederick II comes into the chapel where the bones of the saint-emperor lie in the great golden Karlsschrein, wrought like a church of gold. The new king of the Romans takes hammer and nails and with his own hand drives the last nails home, sealing Charlemagne into the shrine forever. The circle closes: crowned unawares by a pope, he is nailed into gold by an emperor's hand. There he lies to this day under the octagon: the bearded Charles of the Chanson, France's and the empire's dream of the just king, seated, waiting, the Gospel open on his knees.
